opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been a pretty wild shift to live through. When I was a kid in the early seventies I was reading science fiction and books like Feinberg's *The Prometheus Project*, and the idea that we'd build machines smarter than people seemed obvious to me. It was just a question of when. But in mainstream culture it was fringe, something for sci-fi fans and a few eccentric scientists. If you brought it up with ordinary adults, they'd look at you like you were talking about flying saucers.

Through the eighties and nineties it stayed marginal. Even in the 2000s, when Ray Kurzweil, Eliezer Yudkowsky and I were talking about the Singularity and AGI, most of the academic AI field considered it unserious. I coined, or at least popularized, the term "AGI" partly because "AI" had come to mean narrow problem-solving, and the original ambition of thinking machines had become almost embarrassing to say out loud.

Then ChatGPT came along and suddenly everyone's grandmother has talked to a machine that can hold a conversation, write poetry and explain quantum mechanics, badly sometimes, but convincingly. That changed people's intuitions overnight in a way no argument could. Now heads of state, CEOs and regular people at the pub are asking when we'll get human-level AI and what happens after. The Overton window just blew wide open.

My feelings about it are mixed. It's gratifying that the ideas a few of us were pushing for decades are now taken seriously. But the public conversation has jumped from "this is silly" to "this is imminent and maybe terrifying" without spending much time on the nuanced middle. Many people now equate large language models with AGI. I don't think LLMs alone will get us there. They're an amazing component, but you need more cognitive architecture around them for real general intelligence. And the cultural acceptance has come bundled with a lot of concentration of power in a few big tech companies, which worries me more than the technology itself.

So culturally, we've gone from superhuman intelligence being a nerdy fantasy to being a mainstream concern in about fifty years, with most of that change in the last few. The challenge now is to turn that attention into wise action: making sure the path to AGI and beyond is open, decentralized and oriented toward broad benefit, rather than just a race among a few players.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT changed ordinary people’s intuitions and that superhuman AI went from fringe to a mainstream concern, communicating that it has lost its former shock value.

r002.rationale: It describes the idea as obvious to the speaker but fringe in mainstream culture, citing science fiction and eccentric scientists; it does not say early 1970s arguments came from reasonably mainstream, credible sources.

r003.rationale: The response describes a shift over roughly fifty years and says ideas were pushed for decades, but it does not identify credible publication as the starting point of that long path to cultural dominance.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's been a pretty wild ride, honestly. When I first got into this stuff — I was a kid in the early seventies reading science fiction, and then as a teenager getting into the actual AI literature — the idea of a superhuman AI was something you talked about in a science fiction novel, or maybe among a small group of weird people at a university who were considered a bit cranky. Even within the AI field itself, which was already struggling for respectability after the first AI winter, if you said you wanted to build a machine smarter than people, that was a good way to not get your grant funded and to be considered a bit of a nut.

And that persisted for a remarkably long time. I mean, when I coined the term AGI, or rather when we pulled it together with Shane Legg and Cassio Pennachin for that book around 2005, the whole point was to carve out a space to even talk about this, because "AI" had come to mean narrow task-specific software. The mainstream of the field had essentially given up on the original dream of thinking machines and was building spam filters and chess programs. So AGI was a fringe thing, Singularity talk was a fringe thing, and if you brought it up in polite academic company you'd get a kind of amused tolerance at best.

What's happened since ChatGPT is really striking, because the shift wasn't gradual — it was more like a phase transition. In the span of about a year, you went from a world where talking about human-level or superhuman AI got you labeled a crank, to a world where the CEOs of the biggest tech companies on the planet, and heads of state, and the Pope for that matter, are talking about superintelligence as something that may arrive within a decade. The Overton window didn't just shift, it got blown open.

Now, I'd say the acceptance is somewhat shallow in an interesting way. A lot of people now accept that superhuman intelligence is coming, but they haven't really thought through what that means. They treat it like a bigger, better chatbot, or like a somewhat more powerful version of the tools they already have. Whereas the folks who were thinking about this in the seventies and eighties and nineties — the Vinges and the Moravecs and the Kurzweils and the Yudkowskys and so on — were grappling with the fact that a mind qualitatively beyond human is a genuinely different kind of thing. The culture has accepted the word but not quite the concept yet.

And there's a second irony, which is that a lot of the acceptance came through a technology, large language models, that I don't think is going to get us all the way there on its own. So we have this cultural moment where the thing is finally taken seriously, but the mental model most people have of it is shaped by a particular architecture that is kind of a narrow window into what general intelligence could be. In a way we've gone from "this is impossible and you're crazy" to "this is inevitable and it looks like ChatGPT," and both of those are sort of wrong in different ways. But I'll take the second kind of wrong over the first — it's a lot more fun to argue with people who think you're too conservative than with people who think you're insane.

r001.rationale: The response describes a rapid shift since ChatGPT from superhuman AI being treated as crankish to many people accepting it as imminent, while noting that this acceptance is shallow.

r002.rationale: The response characterizes early-1970s discussion as science fiction or the work of a small, crankish group, not arguments available from reasonably mainstream, credible sources.

r003.rationale: The response says the idea remained fringe for a long time, but does not clearly describe a progression from credible publication to cultural dominance.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there’s been a huge shift in what people regard as a serious possibility. In the early 1970s, superhuman intelligence was something you could explore in science fiction, or discuss among a relatively small group of people thinking about AI and the future. It wasn’t generally part of ordinary conversations about where society was going.

Since ChatGPT, that’s changed dramatically. People can interact with a system that does things they had assumed required a human mind. That doesn’t establish that it’s generally intelligent, much less superhuman, but it makes the possibility of more advanced intelligence much less abstract. You don’t have to persuade someone to imagine the entire thing from scratch anymore.

I’d distinguish acceptance of the possibility from enthusiasm about it, though. Someone can now take superhuman AI seriously and be terrified of it, or excited by it, or both. What’s changed is that the discussion increasingly starts with, “What would this mean for us?” rather than, “Why are you talking about science fiction?”

r001.rationale: It contrasts superhuman intelligence as fringe or science fiction in the early 1970s with people now taking the possibility seriously and discussing its implications, communicating reduced shock value.

r002.rationale: The response describes early discussion as limited to a small group; it does not say arguments were available from reasonably mainstream, credible sources.

r003.rationale: It does not observe that ideas can take a long time to move from credible publication to cultural dominance.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, in the early 1970s, the idea of a machine becoming smarter than a human was something you could explore in science fiction, but it wasn’t part of most people’s practical picture of the future. If you took it seriously as something we might actually build, you were pretty far outside the mainstream.

Over time, that changed, although not in a straight line. Computers became normal, the internet became normal, and AI kept producing things that would once have seemed extraordinary. But you could still talk about superhuman intelligence and have people regard it as a rather abstract speculation.

Since ChatGPT, there’s been a shift in the nature of the conversation. People can interact with a system that does at least some of the things they associate with intelligence. That doesn’t establish that it’s generally intelligent, or that simply scaling it up will get us there. But it makes the possibility much more concrete.

So the question has moved from ‘Is this a ridiculous thing to think about?’ toward ‘How far can this go, how soon, and what does it mean for us?’ And cultural acceptance doesn’t necessarily mean enthusiasm. Someone can believe superhuman AI is coming and be terrified of it. What’s changed is that a much broader range of people now regard it as a real possibility.

r001.rationale: The response says superhuman intelligence moved from an idea outside the mainstream to a concrete possibility regarded as real by a much broader range of people since ChatGPT.

r002.rationale: It says taking machine superhuman intelligence seriously in the early 1970s put someone far outside the mainstream, rather than saying credible, reasonably mainstream arguments were already available.

r003.rationale: It describes gradual changes over time, but does not state that ideas can take a long time to move from credible publication to cultural dominance.
